old_title: Booker prize 2026: ask our books team anything about this year's contenders
new_title: 'Why no female lead characters this year?': The Guardian's book team answered your questions
old_text:
For today's reader Q&A we'll be discussing the newly announced shortlist for the 2026 Booker prize which was revealed last night at a discussion at London's Southbank centre featuring this year's judging panel: Jarvis Cocker, Mary Beard, Patricia Lockwood, Raymond Antrobus and the Guardian's own Rebecca Liu.
The panel's final six selections for 2026 are:
The End of Everything by M John Harrison (Serpent's Tail)
The Disappearers by Marlon James (Hamish Hamilton)
Black Bag by Luke Kennard (John Murray)
May We Feed the King by Rebecca Perry (Granta)
The Things We Never Say by Elizabeth Strout (Viking)
John of John by Douglas Stuart (Picador)
The winner will be announced on 9 November 2026 at a ceremony at Old Billingsgate in London.
Liese Spencer and Charlotte Northedge are the Guardian's joint head of books. Justine Jordan is the Guardian's fiction editor and was a Booker judge in 2024, a task for which she had to 150 books in a row (her top tip for doing so was: "put your phone in a different room").
Discuss the shortlist below and/or post a question for Liese, Charlotte and Justine.
Sign in or sign up now to join the conversation.

'Why no female lead characters this year?': The Guardian's book team answered your questions
This year's shortlist for the Booker prize was announced last night. Our books editors answered your questions about the contenders, the judges and literary fiction
We're signing off now. Thanks so much for all the interesting questions. It's been great to see so much enthusiasm for books and for this shortlist in particular - may the best novel win!
TheWildKindness asks: Is the Booker still weighted in favour of major publishers. As I understand it, it's very expensive for indie presses to go through to the shortlist.
Justine: In 2019 the shortlisting of Lucy Ellmann's Ducks, Newburyport caused terrible financial problems for the tiny indie Galley Beggar. I'm not sure if the prize has addressed structural financial issues since then, but it's inevitably weighted towards major publishers because it rewards past success - in the quota system for entries, you can make more submissions if you've had longlistings in the past.
But there is also the 'call in list', where publishers can pitch additional books. And every publisher gets at least one shot - which they know will be seen by five judges. In that sense there's always the chance for small publishers to break through.
We're signing off now. Thanks so much for all the interesting questions. It's been great to see so much enthusiasm for books and for this shortlist in particular - may the best novel win!
Does the Booker shortlist help nudge people toward newer literary fiction?
Hoppo asks: How much do you think the Booker shortlist acts to help nudge people towards newer literary fiction, as against popular fiction or long established classics? I've read a lot more recent literature through the medium of Dua Lipa's book podcast, although the Guardian's 100 greatest novels list is a real pull in the opposite direction!
Liese: I think one of the really cheering developments in recent years is how much the conversation around books has exploded! There are many excellent podcasts, as well as Booktokkers such as Jack Edwards and Booktubers like Eric Karl Anderson who share their favourite reading with millions on social media. These new tastemakers don't only champion recent literary novels but also help to introduce forgotten classics to a whole new readership - see the boom in sales for Dostoevsky's previously obscure novella White Nights. However, I do think that in terms of contemporary literary fiction there remains a really important role for the Booker. Partly because it assesses a vast number of books, partly because it offers the considered choices of an expert panel (rather than just the choices of one influencer) and partly because it is so well established that many people will use it to decide on which new novel to read next. Of course when it comes to deciding on which classic to add to your TBR pile you can't beat our 100 greatest novels list.
DukeApricot asks: Has there ever been a year, or could you envisage there ever being a year, when the judging panel decided that none of the books submitted make the grade? Or at least admitted "X won, but it was a dire year for literary fiction".
Justine: I'm an enthusiast for fiction, and I can't imagine a year that doesn't have 13 (or 12 - judges can also choose a long list of 12, but why would you not use one of your slots?) worthwhile novels in it. I've no on-the-record data about this, but the sense I've developed over the years from amorphous gossip is that there are usually about 30ish strong contenders from which to draw the long list, and that was our experience in 2024. Chair of judges Roddy Doyle was quite grumpy about the general quality last year, but happy to stand by the long list.
Is May We Feed the King too meagre to be worth the read?
LucyIngram asks: Is it worth reading May We Feed the King, or is it one of those annoyingly meagre books that thinks a lack of detail is somehow profound?
Charlotte: I would say it's definitely worth reading May We Feed the King - and it certainly doesn't lack detail. The descriptions of the curator's historical reconstructions are so vivid you can almost feel the weight of the fake apples. It's relatively short, yes, but it really packs a punch. Perhaps by lack of detail you mean specificity about time and place and perspective? In which case, yes, it can be a fairly destabilising read in places. But that's very artfully done, and to my mind, adds to the reading experience. You can get a great overview of it from our excellent review, by Melissa Harrison, who concludes that "it richly rewards those who approach it with curiosity".
Iforgotmynameagain asks: How are the judges chosen? Jarvis Cocker in particular seems like a very left-field choice, do judges apply for the job or are they headhunted?
Justine: An alchemical process of juggling possible names and then approaching people, usually. Though Sarah Jessica Parker, a judge last year, apparently wrote "O let me try!" on an Instagram post about the 2022 judges. "Shall we get our people to talk to your people?" Booker replied, and lo, three years later it came to pass.
Celebrity stardust is obviously important for getting attention for the prize, and there's always been a celeb on each panel. Joanna Lumley did it in 1985 (which didn't go well). Jarvis is a great storyteller, and the kind of guy whose bookshelves you'd be interested in nosing around, which seems a good reason for inclusion.
It's a shame Switzy and Shadow of the Object weren't picked
Kohtao says: Can't believe the two best books - Switzy and Shadow of the Object - were cut. Huge shame as they really added something different to the range.
Liese: I was sad not to see Switzy on the shortlist too. I am a big fan of Emma Cline's writing and felt that it did something really interesting. I am sure that, as always, there were plenty of arguments and some horse-trading among the judges to arrive at this list - which does still include ambitious and experimental work such as The Disappearers (Marlon James) and one of my other faves, the brilliantly weird Black Bag.
Petherick asks: The common theme of the shortlist is men in crisis and there's only one book with a female lead character (Marnie in The End of Everything - I don't think the curator in May We Feed the King is gendered in the book itself and the king is the lead). Do you agree the female perspective is lacking this year and, if so, why?
Charlotte: It's interesting that even Jarvis Cocker, one of this year's judges, said that he found the male dominance of the list "quite surprising, because generally speaking the male-written books weren't as good as the ones written by women". And it's also surprising in the light of the recent debate around the lack of contemporary novels written by men - there was even a small press, Conduit Books, established last year to focus on new male writers. So perhaps we could say that's succeeded! But in fact, a lot of the men on the list are very long established, and there are two previous winners among them - Marlon James and Douglas Stuart.
I would say that although the perspectives are predominantly male, they're not necessarily similar in other ways - they encompass different sexualities, and as you say, one isn't gendered at all (funnily enough, I hadn't read it that way, but others on the desk did and that's obviously how it was intended). It's interesting that we have a female author, Elizabeth Strout, writing from a male perspective, and a male author, M John Harrison, writing from a female perspective. Though Harrison's novel isn't entirely from Marnie's perspective, and for me there are many other themes that jump out from these books, beyond masculinity - anxiety about the world and the future, sexuality, history, oppression. As a shortlist, it seems pretty varied to me, and I didn't find that I missed a female perspective when I was reading these books.
RambleCat57 asks: I adored Black Bag and I'm delighted to see it make the shortlist! Absurd and very funny. I see both poet-novelists have made the shortlist, and I'm curious about the link between poetry and literary fiction. Does being a poet first give a novelist an edge? Heightened sensitivity to language, rhythm, word choice, restraint?
Charlotte: I really enjoyed Black Bag too, and I was really pleased to see it on the shortlist. It's so unexpected and funny, and very thought-provoking - a real achievement. It's great to see both Luke Kennard and Rebecca Perry on the shortlist - and perhaps not a surprise to note that there are two poets on the judging panel: Patricia Lockwood and Raymond Antrobus.
But there's no question that poetry and novel-writing feed into one another, though the two forms require lots of very different skills as well. A poet might be able to write beautiful sentences, but sustaining that over hundreds of pages is another thing entirely. And I'm sure there are plenty of novelists who wouldn't want anyone to read their poetry - if they've attempted it at all. If you can do both well enough to get shortlisted for the Booker prize, you must be doing something right!
Petherick asks: I've read the whole longlist for the first time this year (thanks to my local library). Why do you think we've ended up with a relatively conventional shortlist when the longlist was quite left field and experimental for the Booker (thinking of The Vivisectors, Helen of Nowhere, The Renovation, The Shadow of the Object)?
Firstpoet asks: Why are the themes (in summary admittedly) so predictable? Is it that literary fiction reading and writing is increasingly coterie?
Justine: Is it relatively conventional? I'd say it's still one-third joyfully weird - the success of The End of Everything and May We Feed the King has been one of my favourite things in 2026 so far. I was sad to see The Vivisectors go, but it did seem to me to share quite a lot of territory with Helen of Nowhere. The judges mentioned aiming for "range"' at the shortlist event yesterday evening, which makes sense.
To Firstpoet: I wouldn't have predicted Man in Black Leather Bag or Inexplicable Alien Artefacts this year. Inevitably, the shorthand of describing books can seem repetitive and shopworn. Toxic masculinity klaxon! Brexit! Love and loss (ie, everything)! I'd say one definition of a good book is that it can't be summed up, it has to be read in full, and then we get back to issues of time and space.
UninventiveName asks: How possible is it to separate personal thematic or genre preferences from your appreciation of the quality of a novel? Is it even desirable to attempt to do so? I listened to an interview with a judge a couple of years ago who clearly felt the inclusion of an out-and-out science-fiction novel on the longlist was rather outre.
Liese: I think every reader is going to have personal thematic and genre preferences, and that is no different for Booker judges. Having said that, some of my most thrilling reading has happened when I've been surprised by a book from a genre I might not generally have been drawn towards - or when I've discovered a novel that mixes genres in a really interesting way. So I guess that I think it's impossible to separate your preferences from your appreciation of a novel - but such preferences might also bring depth and range to the way that the Booker judges make their selection ... So, for example, in 2018 when Val McDermid was a judge she championed Belinda Bauer's thriller Snap - which may not have made the cut another year. The same year, Nick Drnaso's Sabrina was the first graphic novel to be Booker listed - which may have been the influence of her fellow judge Leanne Shapton, who is herself a graphic novelist, artist and author.
Ultimately perhaps the distinction to be made is between popular, commercial fiction and literary fiction (see Martin MacInnes's longlisting for his very literary sf novel In Ascension in 2023). But maybe that's just a whole other can of worms! See the question on how to define literary fiction...
UninventiveNameasks: What is literary fiction, really? Seems a meaningless term to me.
Charlotte: That's a good question, and one that we discuss on the books desk all the time - we're often trying to fit new novels into neat categories in our books coverage, when in fact you can have a novel that is, for example, sci-fi, dystopian and literary all in one - M John Harrison's The End of Everything is a good example of that. That's a novel that could have appeared in our monthly science fiction and fantasy roundup, but got a standalone review instead, because it was so clearly a book that merited a longer review, and one that people on the desk were excited about. And we've been vindicated, because here it is on the shortlist!
To me, literary fiction really means any novel that has ambitions beyond fitting into a particular genre category. Many novelists write brilliant romantic fiction, or sci-fi, or fantasy and sell lots of copies, and win prizes within those categories. And lots of those books are also literary. But literary fiction in its broadest sense means novels that transcend genre. I'd be interested to know what others think though. Obviously it's a tricky one to pin down.
Alex42 asks: Do we need a single winner at all? Once you're down to the shortlist - or even possibly the longlist - you've hopefully already got a collection of excellent books to cover a range of tastes. What do we really achieve by picking one of them out? This could apply to any award really, but the idea of ranking works of art in any medium always strikes me as quite odd.
Liese: I agree that - looked at one way - ranking works of art is obviously ridiculous. (We had the same conversation around our 100 greatest novels of all time. Given how subjective reading is, there's something silly about saying that White Teeth is better than A Farewell to Arms or The Prime of Miss Jean Brodie beats David Copperfield). But I would say that the point of that exercise and of the Booker prize too is to spark a conversation and draw attention to great literature. For that reason, I'd argue that it is well worth doing. And from my point of view, there absolutely has to be a winner because otherwise the whole exercise is a bit pointless - and it gives one author a huge boost to their career.
When the judges refused to follow the rules and insisted the prize be split between Bernardine Evaristo and Margaret Atwood in 2019 I think the general consensus was that rather than sharing the glory it detracted from both of their achievements (Atwood said afterwards "I kinda don't need the attention").
senoj1 asks: To get down to the shortlist, how do the judges manage to read 163 novels in 180 days, and then make time to discuss their relative merits and whether a book should move forward or be dropped? It's nearly a novel a day every day for 6 months, all done alongside jobs, family duties, and all of life's other demands. Are the rest of us just mere amateurs?
Willduff says: I wonder if this explains why such very slight - in every sense - novels like Orbital and Flesh won the past couple of years. The shortlist looks interesting, though.
Justine: It's a crazy job, but someone's got to do it - and you only have to do it once. When I was on the judging panel in 2024, the year Orbital won, I took a sabbatical from work which helped and just made reading my number one priority for nine months - what a privilege! My day job is looking at novels and deciding what we should review and who we should send the book to so - uniquely - all that reading is what I feel I should really be doing every year anyway. What readers have in common is that the TBR pile never diminishes.
Undeniably, Booker judging is a strange way to read - at great speed, and then repeatedly, up to three times at least for the shortlist - but it does mean you're considering novels in the round, in a snapshot of the publishing year, in a really interesting and fertile way. I've been on judging panels where the books are shared out, so not everybody reads everything, and the Booker USP is definitely the fact that there are five minds directed on every submission.
To Willduff: I'd disagree here, though I would, wouldn't I - Orbital is a Tardis of a book, a lot bigger on the inside. Flesh seemed a strong winner to me, too, it's a novel so utterly committed to its own project (with perhaps a tiny whiff of sentimentality towards the end). Though my favourite of last year's Booker books will always be Andrew Miller's The Land in Winter.
